metadata.adaptation: WriEng selected one evidenced WordNet sense per headword, joined source Chinese lemmas by exact synset, normalized only source grammatical markers, selected and retained real CMU phonemes, added unmodified wordfreq numeric estimates and inherited ECDICT tag facts, and arranged the compilation as JSON. All field-specific upstream notices remain attached. No invented examples, translations, collocations, expert reviews or exam-frequency statistics.

qualityExclusions.anna: Coin-unit homograph may be confused with a common personal name
qualityExclusions.asshole: Unmarked vulgar register requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.august: Adjective noble has no matching final-stress CMU variant; spelling frequency includes the month
qualityExclusions.being: WordNet independent noun homograph of a frequent grammatical form; retain be instead
qualityExclusions.bitch: Unmarked vulgar/derogatory register requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.cinema: Aligned Chinese source lemmas emphasize celluloid material rather than the selected medium sense
qualityExclusions.cunt: Vulgar register requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.despite: Selected noun contempt is not the common preposition measured by the spelling frequency
qualityExclusions.faggot: Derogatory homograph requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.fuck: Vulgar register requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.going: WordNet independent noun homograph of a frequent grammatical form; retain go instead
qualityExclusions.granger: Farmer sense does not justify prioritizing the potentially name-influenced spelling frequency
qualityExclusions.henry: Inductance-unit homograph may be confused with a common personal name
qualityExclusions.nigger: Racial slur requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.pants: WordNet 3.0 only offers women's underpants for this spelling, inappropriate as a US trousers default
qualityExclusions.shit: Vulgar register requires a separate teaching treatment
qualityExclusions.years: WordNet's independent lemma is old age, while common spelling frequency mostly includes plural year

editorialChecks.review: Automated import plus independent AI-assisted spot checks; not a claim of full professional review

articulate.reason: Prefer putting into words over anatomical joint connection

mobile.reason: Prefer moving/capable of moving over migratory for a general-learning sense

van.reason: Prefer enclosed cargo truck over avant-garde homograph

metadata.examplePolicy: Only quoted examples actually present in the selected WordNet synset, if any. No invented translation, context card, mnemonic or collocation. Synonyms remain distinct from collocations.
metadata.frequencyScope: General English spelling/headword-level mixed-corpus estimate, aggregated across senses and POS; never a count or rank of the selected WordNet meaning
metadata.license: CC-BY-SA-4.0 compilation/frequency derivative; upstream WordNet, COW, CMUdict and MIT tag notices retained per field
metadata.pronunciationPolicy: Exact CMU North American ARPABET phoneme portions, inline comments excluded; only legal 39-phoneme sequences with primary-stress evidence included. Valid source variants retained. Explicit reviewed POS/sense selections correct known heteronyms; remaining first variants are not certified sense-specific. No dictionary IPA imported, no generated audio or pronunciation score, professional review pending.
metadata.review: source-data import and structural validation; independent professional linguistic review pending

routePolicy.daily: Editorial general-frequency core for everyday learning; not a measured US-conversation list
routePolicy.exams: Only exact inherited ECDICT ielts/toefl/cet6/gre tags, as community learning references. Not verified current official syllabuses, exam counts, ranks or guarantees.

metadata.scope: General-English bilingual dictionary core; not a US-spoken or exam-frequency corpus

selection.policy: Lowercase single words 2-24 letters. Choose the highest WordNet sense-use count, then sense number and POS deterministically, before requiring same-synset Chinese, real CMU phonemes and nonzero wordfreq. Exclude reviewed function-word homographs, ambiguous inflected noun/verb forms except lexical plurals, and marked sensitive glosses. Sort eligible headwords by actual general term-level Zipf descending; do not pad with candidates.

## License

`wordfreq` is freely redistributable under the Apache license (see

license (<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/>).

`wordfreq` contains data extracted from Google Books Ngrams
(<http://books.google.com/ngrams>) and Google Books Syntactic Ngrams
(<http://commondatastorage.googleapis.com/books/syntactic-ngrams/index.html>).
The terms of use of this data are:

    Ngram Viewer graphs and data may be freely used for any purpose, although
    acknowledgement of Google Books Ngram Viewer as the source, and inclusion
    of a link to http://books.google.com/ngrams, would be appreciated.

`wordfreq` also contains data derived from the following Creative Commons-licensed
sources:

- The Leeds Internet Corpus, from the University of Leeds Centre for Translation
  Studies (<http://corpus.leeds.ac.uk/list.html>)

- Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (<http://www.wikipedia.org>)

- ParaCrawl, a multilingual Web crawl (<https://paracrawl.eu>)

It contains data from OPUS OpenSubtitles 2018
(<http://opus.nlpl.eu/OpenSubtitles.php>), whose data originates from the
OpenSubtitles project (<http://www.opensubtitles.org/>) and may be used with
attribution to OpenSubtitles.

It contains data from various SUBTLEX word lists: SUBTLEX-US, SUBTLEX-UK,
SUBTLEX-CH, SUBTLEX-DE, and SUBTLEX-NL, created by Marc Brysbaert et al.
(see citations below) and available at
<http://crr.ugent.be/programs-data/subtitle-frequencies>.

I (Robyn Speer) have obtained permission by e-mail from Marc Brysbaert to
distribute these wordlists in wordfreq, to be used for any purpose, not just
for academic use, under these conditions:

- Wordfreq and code derived from it must credit the SUBTLEX authors.
- It must remain clear that SUBTLEX is freely available data.

These terms are similar to the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike license.

Some additional data was collected by a custom application that watches the
streaming Twitter API, in accordance with Twitter's Developer Agreement &
Policy. This software gives statistics about words that are commonly used on
Twitter; it does not display or republish any Twitter content.

## Citing wordfreq

If you use wordfreq in your research, please cite it! We publish the code
through Zenodo so that it can be reliably cited using a DOI. The current
citation is:

> Robyn Speer. (2022). rspeer/wordfreq: v3.0 (v3.0.2). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7199437

The same citation in BibTex format:
